newsitem.title: USA: CBOT corn soars as funds build long positions.
newsitem.headline: CBOT corn soars as funds build long positions.

text.p: Commodity funds switched gears in the corn market on Tuesday, buying at least 80 million bushels of various contract months to counter their recent bias to the short side, analysts and floor traders said.
But market-watchers also said they expected the new-found fund buying would be short-lived due to bearish fundamentals.
"I think farmer selling will limit the rally here," said John Zanutto, head of commercial grain for LFG LLC.
"They're going to let some of it go," Zanutto added. "Don't forget that South America (crops) will come in here and they have the ability to steal some business from the U.S."

Chicago Board of Trade corn futures rallied sharply on Tuesday after a three-day holiday weekend, led by fund buying. Corn closed 10-1/4 to five cents a bushel higher with March up 8-3/4 cents at $2.82-3/4 and May up 10-1/4 cents at $2.84.
"They are in the process of flipping their position now from net short to net long," said Charlie Sernatinger, grain market analyst with E.D. and F. Man International.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission's Commitment of Traders report on Friday, showing positions of large traders, indicated "non-commercials," which included funds, were short corn 215.655 million bushels and long 131.415 million bushels.
Those figures were as of the close Tuesday, February 11.
"The CFTC report on Friday showed (funds) shorter than we thought they were going to be," said Dale Gustafson, analyst with Smith Barney. "They've started to shift to a long position."
When March corn futures rallied above $2.78 per bushel early on Tuesday, the highest level since October 30, the chart-watching funds entered the market as aggressive buyers, Zanutto said.
"We took out $2.78 and technicians were quick to pull the trigger," Zanutto said.
"The move above the recent highs presented a very positive chart, and I don't think the funds wanted to be short," said Steve Freed, analyst with ADM Investor Services.

But Freed and others pointed to overriding fundamental factors that would likely cap gains. The U.S. Department of Agriculture, in its February crop report, pegged U.S. ending corn stocks at 959 million bushels, far above tight 1995-96 ending stocks of 426 million.
Some analysts have suggested U.S. farmers will grow a hefty 9.6 million bushels of corn this year.
USDA will release its initial planting intentions estimates in March and funds will likely bail out of the long positions before then, analysts said.

Meanwhile, USDA upped its estimate for Argentine corn production to 14.5 million tonnes from 13.5 million estimated in January's crop report. Argentina produced 11.1 million tonnes of corn in 1996, USDA said.

FIMAT Futures analyst Dan Cekander agreed that the fund demand was triggered by a technical signal rather than any fundamental supply/demand news. But he said funds would likely add to the long positions this week.
"They usually buy more than one day when they're going from a short to a long like this," Cekander said. "They typically like to get long in the springtime coming into the weather market."
